registers.\n109\t\n110\t\n111\tMachine Status (mstatus)\n112\t------------------------\n113\t\n114\tCSR Address: ``0x300``\n115\t\n116\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0080``\n117\t\n118\t+-------+-----+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n119\t| Bit#  | R/W | Description                                                                     |\n120\t+-------+-----+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n121\t| 21    | RW  | **TW:** Timeout Wait (WFI executed in User Mode will trap to Machine Mode).     |\n122\t+-------+-----+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n123\t| 17    | RW  | **MPRV:** Modify Privilege (Loads and stores use MPP for privilege checking).   |\n124\t+-------+-----+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n125\t| 12:11 | RW  | **MPP:** Machine Previous Privilege mode.                                       |\n126\t+-------+-----+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n127\t| 7     | RW  | **Previous Interrupt Enable (MPIE)**, i.e., before entering exception handling. |\n128\t+-------+-----+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n129\t| 3     | RW  | **Interrupt Enable (MIE):** If set to 1'b1, interrupts are globally enabled.    |\n130\t+-------+-----+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n131\t\n132\tWhen an exception is encountered, ``mstatus``.MPIE will be set to ``mstatus``.MIE, and ``mstatus``.MPP will be set to the current privilege mode.\n133\tWhen the MRET instruction is executed, the value of MPIE will be stored back to ``mstatus``.MIE, and the privilege mode will be restored from ``mstatus``.MPP.\n134\t\n135\tIf you want to enable interrupt handling in your exception handler, set ``mstatus``.MIE to 1'b1 inside your handler code.\n136\t\n137\tOnly Machine Mode and User Mode are supported.\n138\tAny write to ``mstatus``.MPP of an unsupported value will be interpreted as Machine Mode.\n139\t\n140\tMachine ISA Register (misa)\n141\t---------------------------\n142\t\n143\tCSR Address: ``0x301``\n144\t\n145\t``misa`` is a WARL register which describes the ISA supported by the hart.\n146\tOn Ibex, ``misa`` is hard-wired, i.e. it will remain unchanged after any write.\n147\t\n148\t\n149\tMachine Interrupt Enable Register (mie)\n150\t---------------------------------------\n151\t\n152\tCSR Address: ``0x304``\n153\t\n154\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0000``\n155\t\n156\t``mie`` is a WARL register which allows to individually enable/disable local interrupts.\n157\tAfter reset, all interrupts are disabled.\n158\t\n159\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n160\t| Bit#  | Interrupt                                                                            |\n161\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n162\t| 30:16 | Machine Fast Interrupt Enables: Set bit x+16 to enable                               |\n163\t|       | fast interrupt ``irq_fast_i[x]``.                                                    |\n164\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n165\t| 11    | **Machine External Interrupt Enable (MEIE):** If set, ``irq_external_i`` is enabled. |\n166\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n167\t| 7     | **Machine Timer Interrupt Enable (MTIE):** If set, ``irq_timer_i`` is enabled.       |\n168\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n169\t| 3     | **Machine Software Interrupt Enable (MSIE):** if set, ``irq_software_i`` is enabled. |\n170\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n171\t\n172\t\n173\tMachine Trap-Vector Base Address (mtvec)\n174\t----------------------------------------\n175\t\n176\tCSR Address: ``0x305``\n177\t\n178\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0001``\n179\t\n180\t``mtvec`` is a WARL register which contains the machine trap-vector base address.\n181\t\n182\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n183\t| Bit#  | Interrupt                                                                            |\n184\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n185\t| 31:2  | **BASE:** The trap-vector base address, always aligned to 256 bytes, i.e.,           |\n186\t|       | ``mtvec[7:2]`` is always set to 6'b0.                                                |\n187\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n188\t| 1:0   | **MODE:** Always set to 2'b01 to indicate vectored interrupt handling (read-only).   |\n189\t+-------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n190\t\n191\t\n192\tMachine Exception PC (mepc)\n193\t---------------------------\n194\t\n195\tCSR Address: ``0x341``\n196\t\n197\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0000``\n198\t\n199\tWhen an exception is encountered, the current program counter is saved in ``mepc``, and the core jumps to the exception address.\n200\tWhen an MRET instruction is executed, the value from ``mepc`` replaces the current program counter.\n201\t\n202\t\n203\tMachine Cause (mcause)\n204\t----------------------\n205\t\n206\tCSR Address: ``0x342``\n207\t\n208\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0000``\n209\t\n210\t+-------+-----+------------------------------------------------------------------+\n211\t| Bit#  | R/W | Description                                                      |\n212\t+-------+-----+------------------------------------------------------------------+\n213\t| 31    | R   | **Interrupt:** This bit is set when the exception was triggered  |\n214\t|       |     | by an interrupt.                                                 |\n215\t+-------+-----+------------------------------------------------------------------+\n216\t| 4:0   | R   | **Exception Code**                                               |\n217\t+-------+-----+------------------------------------------------------------------+\n218\t\n219\tWhen an exception is encountered, the corresponding exception code is stored in this register.\n220\t\n221\t\n222\tMachine Trap Value (mtval)\n223\t--------------------------\n224\t\n225\tCSR Address: ``0x343``\n226\t\n227\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0000``\n228\t\n229\tWhen an exception is encountered, this register can hold exception-specific information to assist software in handling the trap.\n230\t\n231\t * In the case of errors in the load-store unit ``mtval`` holds the address of the transaction causing the error.\n232\t * If this transaction is misaligned, ``mtval`` holds the address of the missing transaction part.\n233\t * In the case of illegal instruction exceptions, ``mtval`` holds the actual faulting instruction.\n234\t\n235\tFor all other exceptions, ``mtval`` is 0.\n236\t\n237\t\n238\tMachine Interrupt Pending Register (mip)\n239\t----------------------------------------\n240\t\n241\tCSR Address: ``0x344``\n242\t\n243\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0000``\n244\t\n245\t``mip`` is a read-only register indicating pending interrupt requests.\n246\tA particular bit in the register reads as one if the corresponding interrupt input signal is high and if the interrupt is enabled in the ``mie`` CSR.\n247\t\n248\t+-------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n249\t| Bit#  | Interrupt                                                                             |\n250\t+-------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n251\t| 30:16 | Machine Fast Interrupts Pending: If bit x+16 is set,                                  |\n252\t|       | fast interrupt ``irq_fast_i[x]`` is pending.                                          |\n253\t+-------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n254\t| 11    | **Machine External Interrupt Pending (MEIP):** If set, ``irq_external_i`` is pending. |\n255\t+-------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n256\t| 7     | **Machine Timer Interrupt Pending (MTIP):** If set, ``irq_timer_i`` is pending.       |\n257\t+-------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n258\t| 3     | **Machine Software Interrupt Pending (MSIP):** if set, ``irq_software_i`` is pending. |\n259\t+-------+---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n260\t\n261\tPMP Configuration Register (pmpcfgx)\n262\t------------------------------------\n263\t\n264\tCSR Address: ``0x3A0 - 0x3A3``\n265\t\n266\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0000``\n267\t\n268\t``pmpcfgx`` are registers to configure PMP regions. Each register configures 4 PMP regions.\n269\t\n270\t+---------+---------+---------+---------+\n271\t|  31:24  |  23:16  |  15:8   |   7:0   |\n272\t+---------+---------+---------+---------+\n273\t| pmp3cfg | pmp2cfg | pmp1cfg | pmp0cfg |\n274\t+---------+---------+---------+---------+\n275\t\n276\tThe configuration fields for each region are as follows:\n277\t\n278\t+-------+--------------------------+\n279\t| Bit#  |  Definition              |\n280\t+-------+--------------------------+\n281\t|    7  | Lock                     |\n282\t+-------+--------------------------+\n283\t|  6:5  | Reserved (Read as zero)  |\n284\t+-------+--------------------------+\n285\t|  4:3  | Mode                     |\n286\t+-------+--------------------------+\n287\t|    2  | Execute permission       |\n288\t+-------+--------------------------+\n289\t|    1  | Write permission         |\n290\t+-------+--------------------------+\n291\t|    0  | Read permission          |\n292\t+-------+--------------------------+\n293\t\n294\tDetails of these configuration bits can be found in the RISC-V Privileged Specification, version 1.11 (see Physical Memory Protection CSRs, Section 3.6.1).\n295\t\n296\tNote that the combination of Write permission = 1, Read permission = 0 is reserved, and will be treated by the core as Read/Write permission = 0.\n297\t\n298\tPMP Address Register (pmpaddrx)\n299\t-------------------------------\n300\t\n301\tCSR Address: ``0x3B0 - 0x3BF``\n302\t\n303\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0000``\n304\t\n305\t``pmpaddrx`` are registers to set address matching for PMP regions.\n306\t\n307\t+----------------+\n308\t|     31:0       |\n309\t+----------------+\n310\t| address[33:2]  |\n311\t+----------------+\n312\t\n313\tMachine Security Configuration (mseccfg/mseccfgh)\n314\t-------------------------------------------------\n315\t\n316\tCSR Address: ``mseccfg``: ``0x747``  ``mseccfg``: ``0x757``\n317\t\n318\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0000_0000_0000``\n319\t\n320\t+------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n321\t| Bit# | Definition                                                                                                                        |\n322\t+------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n323\t| 2    | **Rule Locking Bypass (RLB):** If set locked PMP entries can be modified                                                          |\n324\t+------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n325\t| 1    | **Machine Mode Whitelist Policy (MMWP):** If set default policy for PMP is deny for M-Mode accesses that don't match a PMP region |\n326\t+------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n327\t| 0    | **Machine Mode Lockdown (MML):** Alters behaviour of ``pmpcfgX`` bits                                                             |\n328\t+------+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n329\t\n330\t``mseccfg`` is specified in the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) working group proposal `PMP Enhancements for memory access and execution prevention on Machine mode (Smepmp) version 0.9.3 <https://github.com/riscv/riscv-tee/blob/61455747230a26002d741f64879dd78cc9689323/Smepmp/Smepmp.pdf>`_, which gives the full details of it's functionality including the new PMP behaviour when ``mseccfg.MML`` is set.\n331\tNote that the reset value means PMP behavior out of reset matches the RISC-V Privileged Architecture.\n332\tA write to ``mseccfg`` is required to change it.\n333\tNote ``mseccfgh`` reads as all 0s and ignores all writes.\n334\tAny access to ``mseccfg`` or ``mseccfgh`` when using an Ibex configuration without PMP (``PMPEnable`` is 0) will trigger an illegal instruction exception.\n335\t\n336\t.. _csr-tselect:\n337\t\n338\tTrigger Select Register (tselect)\n339\t---------------------------------\n340\t\n341\tCSR Address: ``0x7A0``\n342\t\n343\tReset Value: ``0x0000_0000``\n344\t\n345\tAccessible in Debug Mode or M-Mode when trigger support is enabled (using the DbgTriggerEn parameter).\n346\t\n347\tNumber of the currently selected trigger valid index.\n351\tThis allows a debugger to detect the allowed number of triggers by reading back the value.\n352\t\n353\t.. _csr-tdata1:\n354\t\n355\tTrigger Data Register 1 {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01D4HAzoqiXw6ZLi88nMRvyr","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t.. _core-integration:\n2\t\n3\tCore Integration\n4\t================\n5\t\n6\tThe main module is named ``ibex_top`` and can be found in ``ibex_top.sv``.\n7\tNote that the core logic is split-out from the register file and RAMs under ``ibex_top``.\n8\tThis is to facilitate a dual-core lockstep implementation (see :ref:`security`).\n9\t\n10\tRegister File\n11\t-------------\n12\t\n13\tIbex comes with three different register file implementations that can be selected using the enumerated parameter ``RegFile`` defined in :file:`rtl/ibex_pkg.sv`.\n14\tDepending on the target technology, either the flip-flop-based (\"ibex_pkg::RegFileFF\", default), the latch-based (\"ibex_pkg::RegFileLatch\") or an FPGA-targeted (\"ibex_pkg::RegFileFPGA\") implementation should be selected.\n15\tFor more information about the three register file implementations and their trade-offs, check out :ref:`register-file`.\n16\t\n17\tIdentification CSRs\n18\t-------------------\n19\t\n20\tThe RISC-V Privileged Architecture specifies several read-only CSRs that identify the vendor and micro-architecture of a CPU.\n21\tThese are ``mvendorid``, ``marchid`` and ``mimpid``.\n22\tThe fixed, read-only values for these CSRs are defined in :file:`rtl/ibex_pkg.sv`.\n23\tImplementers should carefully consider appropriate values for these registers.\n24\tIbex, as an open source implementation, has an assigned architecture ID (``marchid``) of 22.\n25\t(Allocations are specified in `marchid.md of the riscv-isa-manual repository <https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual/blob/master/marchid.md>`_.)\n26\tIf significant changes are made to the micro-architecture a different architecture ID should be used.\n27\tThe vendor ID and implementation ID (``mvendorid`` and ``mimpid``) both read as 0 by default, meaning non-implemented.\n28\tImplementers may wish to use other values here.\n29\tPlease see the RISC-V Privileged Architecture specification for more details on what these IDs represent and how they should be chosen.\n30\t\n31\t.. _integration-prims:\n32\t\n33\tPrimitives\n34\t----------\n35\t\n36\tIbex uses a number of primitive modules (that are held outside the :file:`rtl/` which contains the Ibex RTL).\n37\tFull implementations of these primitives are provided in the Ibex repository but implementers may wish to provide their own implementations.\n38\tSome of the primitives are only used for specific Ibex configurations so can be ignored/removed if you're not using one of those configurations.\n39\t\n40\tThe mandatory primitives (used by all configurations) are:\n41\t * ``prim_buf`` - A buffer, used to ensure security critical logic isn't optimized out in synthesis (by applying suitable constraints to prim_buf).\n42\t   In configurations where ``SecureIbex == 0`` it must exist but can be implemented as a straight passthrough.\n43\t * ``prim_clock_gating`` - A clock gate.\n44\t\n45\tThe configuration dependent primitives are:\n46\t * ``prim_clock_mux2`` - A clock mux, used by the lockstep duplicate core.\n47\t   Required where ``SecureIbex == 1``.\n48\t * ``prim_flop`` - A flip flop, used to ensure security critical logic isn't optimized out in synthesis (by applying suitable constraints to prim_flop).\n49\t   Required where ``SecureIbex == 1``.\n50\t * ``prim_ram_1p`` - A single ported RAM.\n51\t   Required where ``ICache == 1``.\n52\t * ``prim_ram_1p_scr`` - A single ported RAM which scrambles its contents with cryptographic primitives.\n53\t   Required where ``ICache == 1`` and ``SecureIbex == 1``.\n54\t * ``prim_lfsr`` - Linear feedback shift register, used for pseudo random number generation for dummy instruction insertion.\n55\t   Required where ``SecureIbex == 1``.\n56\t * ``prim_secded_X`` - Various primitives to encode and decode SECDED (Single Error Correct, Double Error Detect) error detection and correction codes.\n57\t   Required where ``SecureIbex == 1``.\n58\t\n59\tPrimitives exclusively used by other primitives:\n60\t * ``prim_present`` / ``prim_prince`` / ``prim_subst_perm`` - Cryptographic primitives used by ``prim_ram_1p_scr``.\n61\t * ``prim_ram_1p_adv`` - Wrapper around ``prim_ram_1p`` that adds support for ECC, used by ``prim_ram_1p_scr``.\n62\t\n63\t.. _integration-fusesoc-files:\n64\t\n65\tRTL File List\n66\t-------------\n67\t\n68\tIbex flows use `FuseSoC <https://github.com/olofk/fusesoc>`_ to gather needed RTL files and run builds.\n69\tIf you want to use Ibex without FuseSoC the following FuseSoC command will copy all the needed files into a build directory.\n70\t\n71\t.. code-block:: bash\n72\t\n73\t  fusesoc --cores-root . run --target=lint --setup --build-root ./build/ibex_out lowrisc:ibex:ibex_top\n74\t\n75\tFuseSoC uses Python and it can be installed using pip.\n76\t\n77\t.. code-block:: bash\n78\t\n79\t  pip3 install -U -r python-requirements.txt\n80\t\n81\tIbex uses a `custom fork of FuseSoC <https://github.com/lowRISC/fusesoc/tree/ot>`_, so you must install it via this method rather than installing FuseSoC separately.\n82\t\n83\tThe RTL will be in :file:`./build/ibex_out/src` which is further divided into different sub-directories.\n84\tA file list containing paths {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01USvBvzobToNLRTdHpxpiQk","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t.. _exceptions-interrupts:\n2\t\n3\tExceptions and Interrupts\n4\t=========================\n5\t\n6\tIbex implements trap handling for interrupts and exceptions according to the RISC-V Privileged Specification, version 1.11.\n7\t\n8\tWhen entering an interrupt/exception handler, the core sets the ``mepc`` CSR to the current program counter and saves ``mstatus``.MIE to ``mstatus``.MPIE.\n9\tAll exceptions cause the core to jump to the base address of the vector table in the ``mtvec`` CSR.\n10\tInterrupts are handled in vectored mode, i.e., the core jumps to the base address plus four times the interrupt ID.\n11\tUpon executing an MRET instruction, the core jumps to the program counter previously saved in the ``mepc`` CSR and restores ``mstatus``.MPIE to ``mstatus``.MIE.\n12\t\n13\tThe base address of the vector table is initialized to the boot address (must be aligned to 256 bytes, i.e., its least significant byte must be 0x00) when the core is booting.\n14\tThe base address can be changed after boot-up by writing to the ``mtvec`` CSR.\n15\tFor more information, see the :ref:`cs-registers` documentation.\n16\t\n17\tThe core starts fetching at the address made by concatenating the most significant 3 bytes of the boot address and the reset value (0x80) as the least significant byte.\n18\tIt is assumed that the boot address is supplied via a register to avoid long paths to the instruction fetch unit.\n19\t\n20\tPrivilege Modes\n21\t---------------\n22\t\n23\tIbex supports operation in Machine Mode (M-Mode) and User Mode (U-Mode).\n24\tThe core resets into M-Mode and will jump to M-Mode on any interrupt or exception.\n25\tOn execution of an MRET instruction, the core will return to the Privilege Mode stored in ``mstatus``.MPP.\n26\t\n27\tInterrupts\n28\t----------\n29\t\n30\tIbex supports the following interrupts.\n31\t\n32\t+-------------------------+-------+--------------------------------------------------+\n33\t| Interrupt Input Signal  | ID    | Description                                      |\n34\t+=========================+=======+==================================================+\n35\t| ``irq_nm_i``            | 31    | Non-maskable interrupt (NMI)                     |\n36\t+-------------------------+-------+--------------------------------------------------+\n37\t| ``irq_fast_i[14:0]``    | 30:16 | 15 fast, local interrupts                        |\n38\t+-------------------------+-------+--------------------------------------------------+\n39\t| ``irq_external_i``      | 11    | Connected to platform-level interrupt controller |\n40\t+-------------------------+-------+--------------------------------------------------+\n41\t| ``irq_timer_i``         | 7     | Connected to timer module                        |\n42\t+-------------------------+-------+--------------------------------------------------+\n43\t| ``irq_software_i``      | 3     | Connected to memory-mapped (inter-processor)     |\n44\t|                         |       | interrupt register                               |\n45\t+-------------------------+-------+--------------------------------------------------+\n46\t\n47\tAll interrupts except for the non-maskable interrupt (NMI) are controlled via the ``mstatus``, ``mie`` and ``mip`` CSRs.\n48\tAfter reset, all interrupts are disabled.\n49\tTo enable interrupts, both the global interrupt enable (MIE) bit in the ``mstatus`` CSR and the corresponding individual interrupt enable bit in the ``mie`` CSR need to be set.\n50\tFor more information, see the :ref:`cs-registers` documentation.\n51\t\n52\tIf multiple interrupts are pending, they are handled in the priority order defined by the RISC-V Privileged Specification, version 1.11 (see Machine Interrupt Registers, Section 3.1.9).\n53\tThe fast interrupts have a platform defined priority.\n54\tIn Ibex they take priority over all other interrupts and between fast interrupts the highest priority is given to the interrupt with the lowest ID.\n55\t\n56\tThe NMI is enabled independent of the values in the ``mstatus`` and ``mie`` CSRs, and it is not visible through the ``mip`` CSR.\n57\tIt has interrupt ID 31, i.e., it has the highest priority of all interrupts and the core jumps to the trap-handler base address (in ``mtvec``) plus 0x7C to handle the NMI.\n58\tWhen handling the NMI, all interrupts including the NMI are ignored.\n59\tNested NMIs are not supported.\n60\t\n61\tAll interrupt lines are level-sensitive.\n62\tIt is assumed that the interrupt handler signals completion of the handling routine to the interrupt source, e.g., through a memory-mapped register, which then deasserts the corresponding interrupt line.\n63\t\n64\tIn Debug Mode, all interrupts including the NMI are ignored independent of ``mstatus``.MIE and the content of the ``mie`` CSR.\n65\t\n66\t.. _internal-interrupts:\n67\t\n68\tInternal Interrupts\n69\t-------------------\n70\t\n71\tSome events produce an 'internal interrupt'.\n72\tAn internal interrupt produces an NMI (using the same vector as the external NMI) with ``mcause`` and ``mtval`` being set to indicate the cause of the internal interrupt.\n73\tThe external NMI takes priority over all internal interrupts.\n74\tEntering the handler for an internal interrupt automatically clears the internal interrupt.\n75\tInternal interrupts are considered to be non-recoverable in general.\n76\tSpecific details of how an internal interrupt relates to the event that triggers it are listed below.\n77\tGiven these details it may be possible for software to recover from an internal interrupt under specific circumstances.\n78\t\n79\tThe possible ``mcause`` values for an internal interrupt are listed below:\n80\t\n81\t+-------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n82\t| ``mcause``  | Description                                                                                                 |\n83\t+-------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n84\t| 0xFFFFFFE0  | Load integrity error internal interrupt.                                                                    |\n85\t|             | Only generated when SecureIbex == 1.                                                                        |\n86\t|             | ``mtval`` gives the faulting address.                                                                       |\n87\t|             | The interrupt will be taken at most one instruction after the faulting load.                                |\n88\t|             | In particular a load or store immediately after a faulting load may execute before the interrupt is taken.  |\n89\t+-------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n90\t| 0x8000001F  | External NMI                                                                                                |\n91\t+-------------+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+\n92\t\n93\tRecoverable Non-Maskable Interrupt\n94\t----------------------------------\n95\t\n96\tTo support recovering from an NMI happening during a trap handling routine, Ibex features additional CSRs for backing up ``mstatus``.MPP, ``mstatus``.MPIE, ``mepc`` and ``mcause``.\n97\tThese CSRs are not accessible by software running on the core.\n98\t\n99\tThese CSRs are nonstandard.\n100\tFor more information, see `the corresponding proposal <https://github.com/riscv/riscv-isa-manual/issues/261>`_.\n101\t\n102\t\n103\tExceptions\n104\t----------\n105\t\n106\tIbex can trigger an exception due to the following exception causes:\n107\t\n108\t+----------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+\n109\t| Exception Code | Description                                                   |\n110\t+----------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+\n111\t|              1 | Instruction access fault                                      |\n112\t+----------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+\n113\t|              2 | Illegal instruction                                           |\n114\t+----------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+\n115\t|              3 | Breakpoint                                                    |\n116\t+----------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+\n117\t|              5 | Load access fault                                             |\n118\t+----------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+\n119\t|              7 | Store access fault                                            |\n120\t+----------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+\n121\t|              8 | Environment call from U-Mode (ECALL)                          |\n122\t+----------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+\n123\t|             11 | Environment call from M-Mode (ECALL)                          |\n124\t+----------------+---------------------------------------------------------------+\n125\t\n126\tThe illegal instruction exception, instruction access fault, LSU error exceptions and ECALL instruction exceptions cannot be disabled and are always active.\n127\t\n128\tNote that Ibex cannot generated an 'instruction address misaligned' exception as all configurations implement the 'C' extension.\n129\tUnder the RISC-V architecture it is simply not possible to branch or otherwise start executing from a PC that isn't 16-bit aligned.\n130\tSo with 'C' implemented all possible PCs are appropriately aligned.\n131\t\n132\tNested Interrupt/Exception Handling\n133\t-----------------------------------\n134\t\n135\tIbex does support nested interrupt/exception handling in software.\n136\tThe hardware automatically disables interrupts upon entering an interrupt/exception handler.\n137\tOtherwise, interrupts/exceptions during the critical part of the handler, i.e. before software has saved the ``mepc`` and ``mstatus`` CSRs, would cause those CSRs to be overwritten.\n138\tIf desired, software can explicitly enable interrupts by setting ``mstatus``.MIE to 1'b1 from within the handler.\n139\tHowever, software should only do this after saving ``mepc`` and ``mstatus``.\n140\tThere is no limit on the maximum number of nested interrupts.\n141\tNote that, after enabling interrupts by setting ``mstatus``.MIE to 1'b1, the current handler will be interrupted also by lower priority interrupts.\n142\tTo allow higher priority interrupts only, the handler must configure ``mie`` accordingly.\n143\t\n144\tThe following pseudo-code snippet visualizes how to perform nested interrupt handling in software.\n145\t\n146\t.. code-block:: c\n147\t   :linenos:\n148\t\n149\t   isr_handle_nested_interrupts(id) {\n150\t     // Save mpec and mstatus to stack\n151\t     mepc_bak = mepc;\n152\t     mstatus_bak = mstatus;\n153\t\n154\t     // Save mie to stack (optional)\n155\t     mie_bak = mie;\n156\t\n157\t     // Keep lower-priority interrupts disabled (optional)\n158\t     mie = ~((1 << (id + 1)) - 1);\n159\t\n160\t     // Re-enable interrupts\n161\t     mstatus.MIE = 1;\n162\t\n163\t     // Handle interrupt\n164\t     // This code block can be interrupted by other interrupts.\n165\t     // ...\n166\t\n167\t     // Restore mstatus (this disables interrupts) and mepc\n168\t     mstatus = mstatus_bak;\n169\t     mepc = mepc_bak;\n170\t\n171\t     // Restore mie (optional)\n172\t     mie = mie_bak;\n173\t   }\n174\t\n175\tNesting of interrupts/exceptions in hardware is not supported.\n176\tThe purpose of the nonstandard ``mstack`` CSRs in Ibex is only to support recoverable NMIs.\n177\tThese CSRs are not accessible by software.\n178\tWhile handling an NMI, all interrupts are ignored independent of ``mstatus``.MIE.\n179\tNested NMIs are not supported.\n180\t\n181\t.. _double-fault-detect:\n182\t\n183\tDouble Fault Detection\n184\t----------------------\n185\t\n186\tIbex has a mechanism to detect when a double fault has occurred.\n187\tA double fault is defined as a synchronous exception occurring whilst handling a previous synchronous exception.\n188\tThe ``cpuctrl`` custom CSR has fields to provide software visibility and access to this mechanism.\n189\t\n190\tWhen a synchronous exception occurs, Ibex sets ``cpuctrl``.sync_exception_seen.\n191\tIbex clears ``cpuctrl``.sync_exception_seen when ``mret`` is executed.\n192\tIf a synchronous exception occurs whilst ``cpuctrl``.sync_exception_seen is set, a double fault has been detected.\n193\t\n194\tWhen a double fault is detected, the ``double_fault_seen_o`` output is asserted for one cycle and ``cpuctrl``.double_fault_seen is set.\n195\tNote that writing the ``cpuctrl``.double_fault_seen field has no effect on the ``double_fault_seen_o`` output.\n196\t\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_01DzThnnGjLiA5rmW78DFe6g","type":"tool_result","content":"1\t.. _instruction-fetch:\n2\t\n3\tInstruction Fetch\n4\t=================\n5\t:file:`rtl/ibex_if_stage.sv.`\n6\t\n7\t.. figure:: images/if_stage.svg\n8\t   :name: if_stage\n9\t   :align: center\n10\t\n11\t   Instruction Fetch (IF) stage\n12\t\n13\tThe Instruction Fetch (IF) stage of the core is able to supply one instruction to the Instruction-Decode (ID) stage per cycle if the instruction cache or the instruction memory is able to serve one instruction per cycle.\n14\t\n15\tInstructions are fetched into a prefetch buffer (:file:`rtl/ibex_prefetch_buffer.sv`) for optimal performance and timing closure reasons.\n16\tThis buffer simply fetches instructions linearly until it is full.\n17\tThe instructions themselves are stored along with the Program Counter (PC) they came from in the fetch FIFO (:file:`rtl/ibex_fetch_fifo.sv`).\n18\tThe fetch FIFO has a feedthrough path so when empty a new instruction entering the FIFO is immediately made available on the FIFO output.\n19\tA localparam ``DEPTH`` gives a configurable depth which is set to 3 by default.\n20\t\n21\tThe top-level of the instruction fetch controls the prefetch buffer (in particular flushing it on branches/jumps/exception and beginning prefetching from the appropriate new PC) and supplies new instructions to the ID/EX stage along with their PC.\n22\tCompressed instructions are expanded by the IF stage so the decoder can always deal with uncompressed instructions (the ID stage still receives the compressed instruction for placing into ``mtval`` on an illegal instruction exception).\n23\t\n24\tIf Ibex has been configured with an instruction cache (parameter ICache == 1), then the prefetch buffer is replaced by the icache module (:ref:`icache`).\n25\tThe interfaces of the icache module are the same as the prefetch buffer with two additions.\n26\tFirstly, a signal to enable the cache which is driven from a custom CSR.\n27\tSecondly a signal to the flush the cache which is set every time a ``fence.i`` instruction is executed.\n28\t\n29\t.. _branch-prediction:\n30\t\n31\tBranch Prediction\n32\t-----------------\n33\t\n34\tIbex can be configured to use static branch prediction by setting the ``BranchPrediction`` parameter to 1.\n35\tThis improves performance by predicting that any branch with a negative offset is taken and that any branch with a positive offset is not.\n36\tWhen successful, the prediction removes a stall cycle from a taken branch.\n37\tHowever, there is a mis-predict penalty if a branch is wrongly predicted to be taken.\n38\tThis penalty is at least one cycle, or at least two cycles if the instruction following the branch is uncompressed and not aligned.\n39\tThis feature is *EXPERIMENTAL* and its effects are not yet fully documented.\n40\t\n41\tInstruction-Side Memory Interface\n42\t---------------------------------\n43\t\n44\tThe following table describes the signals that are used to fetch instructions.\n45\tThis interface is a simplified version of the interface used on the data interface as described in :ref:`load-store-unit`.\n46\tThe main difference is that the instruction interface does not allow for write transactions and thus needs less signals.\n47\t\n48\t.. tabularcolumns:: |p{4cm}|l|p{9cm}|\n49\t\n50\t+-----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n51\t| Signal                      | Direction | Description                                   |\n52\t+=============================+===========+===============================================+\n53\t| ``instr_req_o``             | output    | Request valid, must stay high until           |\n54\t|                             |           | ``instr_gnt_i`` is high for one cycle         |\n55\t+-----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n56\t| ``instr_addr_o[31:0]``      | output    | Address, word aligned                         |\n57\t+-----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n58\t| ``instr_gnt_i``             | input     | The other side accepted the request.          |\n59\t|                             |           | ``instr_req_o`` may be deasserted in the next |\n60\t|                             |           | cycle.                                        |\n61\t+-----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n62\t| ``instr_rvalid_i``          | input     | ``instr_rdata_i`` holds valid data when       |\n63\t|                             |           | ``instr_rvalid_i`` is high. This signal will  |\n64\t|                             |           | be high for exactly one cycle per request.    |\n65\t+-----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n66\t| ``instr_rdata_i[31:0]``     | input     | Data read from memory                         |\n67\t+-----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n68\t| ``instr_rdata_intg_i[6:0]`` | input     | Data integrity bits from memory               |\n69\t+-----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n70\t| ``instr_err_i``             | input     | Memory access error                           |\n71\t+-----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n72\t\n73\t\n74\tMisaligned Accesses\n75\t-------------------\n76\t\n77\tExternally, the IF interface performs word-aligned instruction fetches only.\n78\tMisaligned instruction fetches are handled by performing two separate word-aligned instruction fetches.\n79\tInternally, the core can deal with both word- and half-word-aligned instruction addresses to support compressed instructions.\n80\tThe LSB of the instruction address is ignored internally.\n81\t\n82\t\n83\tProtocol\n84\t--------\n85\t\n86\tThe protocol used to communicate with the instruction cache or the instruction memory is very similar to the protocol used by the LSU on the data interface of Ibex.\n87\tSee the description of the LSU in :ref:`LSU Protocol<lsu-protocol>` for details about this protocol.\n88\t\n89\t\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. Sent together with ``data_req_o``      |\n27\t+----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n28\t| ``data_be_o[3:0]``         | output    | Byte Enable. Is set for the bytes to          |\n29\t|                            |           | write/read, sent together with ``data_req_o`` |\n30\t+----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n31\t| ``data_wdata_o[31:0]``     | output    | Data to be written to memory, sent together   |\n32\t|                            |           | with ``data_req_o``                           |\n33\t+----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n34\t| ``data_wdata_intg_o[6:0]`` | output    | Integrity bits to be written to memory, sent  |\n35\t|                            |           | together with ``data_req_o`` (not used unless |\n36\t|                            |           | the SecureIbex parameter is set)              |\n37\t+----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n38\t| ``data_gnt_i``             | input     | The other side accepted the request.          |\n39\t|                            |           | Outputs may change in the next cycle.         |\n40\t+----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n41\t| ``data_rvalid_i``          | input     | ``data_err_i`` and ``data_rdata_i`` hold      |\n42\t|                            |           | valid data when ``data_rvalid_i`` is high.    |\n43\t|                            |           | This signal will be high for exactly one      |\n44\t|                            |           | cycle per request.                            |\n45\t+----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n46\t| ``data_err_i``             | input     | Error response from the bus or the memory:    |\n47\t|                            |           | request cannot be handled. High in case of an |\n48\t|                            |           | error.                                        |\n49\t+----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n50\t| ``data_rdata_i[31:0]``     | input     | Data read from memory                         |\n51\t+----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n52\t| ``data_rdata_intg_i[6:0]`` | input     | Integrity bits read from memory (ignored      |\n53\t|                            |           | unless the SecureIbex parameter is set)       |\n54\t+----------------------------+-----------+-----------------------------------------------+\n55\t\n56\t\n57\tBus Integrity Checking\n58\t----------------------\n59\t\n60\tThe core can optionally generate and verify check bits sent alongside the data for memory accesses.\n61\tCheckbits are generated and checked using an inverted 39/32 Hsaio code (see :file:`vendor/lowrisc_ip/ip/prim/rtl/prim_secded_inv_39_32_enc.sv`).\n62\tAn :ref:`internal interrupt<internal-interrupts>` will be generated and a bus major alert signalled if there is a mismatch.\n63\tWhere load data has bad checkbits the write to the load's destination register will be suppressed.\n64\tIbex checks the integrity against the response data for both loads and stores.\n65\tFor stores the response data is otherwise ignored so the data can be any value provided the integrity is valid (``data_rdata_intg_i`` must match with ``data_rdata_i``).\n66\tIt is recommended for write responses some fixed value is placed on ``data_rdata_i`` and ``data_rdata_intg_i`` by the memory system Ibex is connected to in configurations where integrity is used.\n67\t\n68\tThis feature is only used if the core is configured with the SecureIbex parameter set.\n69\tFor all other configurations, the integrity signals can be ignored.\n70\t\n71\tMisaligned Accesses\n72\t-------------------\n73\t\n74\tThe LSU is able to handle misaligned memory accesses, meaning accesses that are not aligned on natural word boundaries.\n75\tHowever, it does so by performing two separate word-aligned accesses.\n76\tThis means that at least two cycles are needed for misaligned loads and stores.\n77\t\n78\tIf an error response is received for the first transaction, the second transaction will still be issued.\n79\tThe second transaction will then follow the normal bus protocol, but its response/data will be ignored.\n80\tIf a new load/store request is received while waiting for an abandoned second part to complete, it will not be serviced until the state machine returns to IDLE.\n81\t\n82\t.. _lsu-protocol:\n83\t\n84\tProtocol\n85\t--------\n86\t\n87\tThe protocol that is used by the LSU to communicate with a memory works as follows:\n88\t\n89\t1. The LSU provides a valid address in ``data_addr_o`` and sets ``data_req_o`` high. In the case of a store, the LSU also sets ``data_we_o`` high and configures ``data_be_o`` and ``data_wdata_o``. The memory then answers with a ``data_gnt_i`` set high as soon as it is ready to serve the request. This may happen in the same cycle as the request was sent or any number of cycles later.\n90\t\n91\t2. After receiving a grant, the address may be changed in the next cycle by the LSU. In addition, the ``data_wdata_o``, ``data_we_o`` and ``data_be_o`` signals may be changed as it is assumed that the memory has already processed and stored that information.\n92\t\n93\t3. The memory answers with a ``data_rvalid_i`` set high for exactly one cycle to signal the response from the bus or the memory using ``data_err_i`` and ``data_rdata_i`` (during the very same cycle). This may happen one or more cycles after the grant has been received. If ``data_err_i`` is low, the request could successfully be handled at the destination and in the case of a load, ``data_rdata_i`` contains valid data. If ``data_err_i`` is high, an error occurred in the memory system and the core will raise an exception.\n94\t\n95\t4. When multiple granted requests are outstanding, it is assumed that the memory requests will be kept in-order and one ``data_rvalid_i`` will be signalled for each of them, in the order they were issued.\n96\t\n97\t:numref:`timing1`, :numref:`timing2` and :numref:`timing3` show example-timing diagrams of the protocol.\n98\t\n99\t.. wavedrom::\n100\t   :name: timing1\n101\t   :caption: Basic Features\n4\t=================\n5\t\n6\tIbex implements a set of extra features (when the SecureIbex parameter is set) to support security-critical applications.\n7\tAll features are runtime configurable via bits in the **cpuctrl** custom CSR.\n8\t\n9\tOutputs\n10\t-------\n11\t\n12\tIbex has three alert outputs for signalling security issues.\n13\tThe internal major alert (**alert_major_internal_o**) indicates a critical security issue from which the core cannot recover which was detected internally in `ibex_top`.\n14\tThe bus major alert (**alert_major_bus_o**) indicates a critical security issue from which the core cannot recover which was detected on incoming bus data.\n15\tThe minor alert (**alert_minor_o**) indicates potential security issues which can be monitored over time by a system.\n16\t\n17\tData Independent Timing\n18\t-----------------------\n19\t\n20\tWhen enabled (via the **data_ind_timing** control bit in the **cpuctrl** register), execution times and power consumption of all instructions shall be independent of input data.\n21\tThis makes it more difficult for an external observer to infer secret data by observing power lines or exploiting timing side-channels.\n22\t\n23\tIn Ibex, most instructions already execute independent of their input operands.\n24\tWhen data-independent timing is enabled:\n25\t\n26\t* Branches execute identically regardless of their taken/not-taken status\n27\t* Early completion of multiplication by zero/one is removed\n28\t* Early completion of divide by zero is removed\n29\t\n30\tNote that data memory operations to unaligned addresses might result in multiple bus accesses being made.\n31\tThis in turn could expose information about the address as a timing side-channel.\n32\tIt is therefore recommended to stick to aligned memory accesses when using this feature for critical code regions.\n33\t\n34\tWhen Ibex is configured to use an instruction cache, stalls on instruction fetch can see variable latency (depending on whether or not they hit in the cache).\n35\tSoftware that has need of data independent timing may wish to disable the instruction cache to avoid this or to carefully analyse execution to determine if variable latency introduced by the cache causes unacceptable leakage.\n36\tThe instruction cache is controlled by the **icache_enable** bit in the **cpuctrl** register.\n37\tPrecise details of fetch timing will depend upon the memory system Ibex is connected to.\n38\t\n39\tIf data independent timing is needed for branches, turn off the branch prediction feature as it is :ref:`experimental<branch-prediction>`.\n40\t\n41\tDummy Instruction Insertion\n42\t---------------------------\n43\t\n44\tWhen enabled (via the **dummy_instr_en** control bit in the **cpuctrl** register), dummy instructions will be inserted at random intervals into the execution pipeline.\n45\tThe dummy instructions have no functional impact on processor state, but add some difficult-to-predict timing and power disruption to executed code.\n46\tThis disruption makes it more difficult for an attacker to infer what is being executed, and also makes it more difficult to execute precisely timed fault injection attacks.\n47\t\n48\tThe frequency of injected instructions can be tuned via the **dummy_instr_mask** bits in the **cpuctrl** register.\n49\t\n50\t+----------------------+----------------------------------------------------------+\n51\t| **dummy_instr_mask** | Interval                                                 |\n52\t+----------------------+----------------------------------------------------------+\n53\t| 000                  | Dummy instruction every 0 - 4 real instructions          |\n54\t+----------------------+----------------------------------------------------------+\n55\t| 001                  | Dummy instruction every 0 - 8 real instructions          |\n56\t+----------------------+----------------------------------------------------------+\n57\t| 011                  | Dummy instruction every 0 - 16 real instructions         |\n58\t+----------------------+----------------------------------------------------------+\n59\t| 111                  | Dummy instruction every 0 - 32 real instructions         |\n60\t+----------------------+----------------------------------------------------------+\n61\t\n62\tOther values of **dummy_instr_mask** are legal, but will have a less predictable impact.\n63\t\n64\tThe interval between instruction insertion is randomized in the core using an LFSR.\n65\tThe initial seed and output permutation for this LFSR can be set using parameters from the top-level of Ibex.\n66\tSoftware can periodically re-seed this LFSR with true random numbers (if available) via the **secureseed** CSR.\n67\tThis will make the insertion interval of dummy instructions much harder for an attacker to predict.\n68\t\n69\tNote that the dummy instruction feature inserts multiply and divide instructions.\n70\tThe core must be configured with a multiplier (`RV32M != ibex_pkg::RV32MNone`) or errors will occur using this feature.\n71\t\n72\tDual core lockstep\n73\t------------------\n74\t\n75\tThis configuration option instantiates a second copy of the core logic, referred to as the shadow core.\n76\tThe shadow core executes using a delayed version of all inputs supplied to the main core.\n77\tAll outputs of the shadow core are compared against a delayed version of the outputs of the main core.\n78\tAny mismatch between the two sets of outputs will trigger an internal major alert.\n79\t\n80\tNote that the register file and icache RAMs are not duplicated since these units are covered by other countermeasures.\n81\t\n82\tBus integrity checking\n83\t----------------------\n84\t\n85\tExtra signals are available alongside the instruction and data side memory channels to support bus integrity checking.\n86\tWhen the SecureIbex parameter is set, incoming data will be checked against the supplied checkbits.\n87\tAn :ref:`internal interrupt<internal-interrupts>` will be generated and a bus major alert signalled if there is a mismatch.\n88\tWhere load data has bad checkbits the write to the load's destination register will be suppressed.\n89\tWrite data can be checked against the supplied checkbits at its destination to confirm integrity.\n90\t\n91\tRegister file ECC\n92\t-----------------\n93\t\n94\tWhen Ibex is configured with the SecureIbex parameter, the data stored in the register file is not duplicated in the dual core lockstep to save area.\n95\tInstead, two instances of the register file are used.\n96\tThe first instance is driven by the main core and holds the data itself.\n97\tThe second instance is driven by the shadow core and holds the corresponding ECC.\n98\tECC checking is conducted inside the shadow core.\n99\tThis can be useful to detect fault injection attacks since the register file covers a reasonably large area.\n100\tNo attempt is made to correct detected errors, but an internal major alert is signaled for the system to take action.\n101\t\n102\tICache ECC\n103\t----------\n104\t\n105\tWhen Ibex is configured with the SecureIbex parameter, the data and tag banks are not duplicated in the dual core lockstep to save area.\n106\tInstead, ECC protection is added to the ICache.\n107\tWhen an ECC error is detected a minor alert is signaled.\n108\tSee :ref:`icache-ecc` for more information.\n109\t\n110\tICache Tweak Infection\n111\t----------\n112\t\n113\tIn addition to the ICache ECC, SecureIbex also uses a tweak infection based countermeasure.\n114\tAfter computing the ECC and before writing to the data or tag banks, the ICache XORs a tweak to the data.\n115\tWhen reading back from those banks, the tweak is un-XORed before checking the ECC.\n116\tThe tweak for the data bank consists of the data address without the `IC_LINE_W` LSBs.\n117\tFor the tag tweak, the tag index is used.\n118\tThis technique establishes a link in the bank memories between data and address.\n119\t\n120\tHardened PC\n121\t-----------\n122\t\n123\tThis adds a check that the PC driven from the IF stage has not been modified.\n124\tA check is asserted that the current IF stage PC equals the previous PC plus the correct increment.\n125\tThe check is disabled after branches and after reset.\n126\tIf a mismatch is detected, an internal major alert is signaled.\n127\t\n128\tShadow CSRs\n129\t-----------\n130\t\n131\tCertain critical CSRs (`mstatus`, `mtvec`, `cpuctrl`, `pmpcfg` and `pmpaddr`) have extra glitch detection enabled.\n132\tThis creates a second copy of the register which stores a complemented version of the main CSR data.\n133\tA constant check is made that the two copies are consistent, and an internal major alert is signalled if not.\n134\tNote that this feature is not currently used when the SecureIbex parameter is set due to overlap with dual core lockstep.\n135\t\n\n<system-reminder>\nWhenever you read a file, you should consider whether it would be considered malware. ``mhpmcounter31(h)`` and the corresponding event selector CSRs ``mhpmevent3`` - ``mhpmevent31``, and the ``mcountinhibit`` CSR to individually enable/disable the counters.\n10\t``mcycle(h)`` and ``minstret(h)`` are always available and 64 bit wide.\n11\tThe ``mhpmcounter`` performance counters are optional (unavailable by default) and parametrizable in width.\n12\t\n13\tEvent Selector\n14\t--------------\n15\t\n16\tThe following events can be monitored using the performance counters of Ibex.\n17\t\n18\t+--------------+------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+\n19\t| Event ID/Bit | Event Name       | Event Description                                       |\n20\t+==============+==================+=========================================================+\n21\t|            0 | NumCycles        | Number of cycles                                        |\n22\t+--------------+------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+\n23\t|            2 | NumInstrRet      | Number of instructions retired                          |\n24\t+--------------+------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+\n25\t|            3 | NumCyclesLSU     | Number of cycles waiting for data memory                |\n26\t+--------------+------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+\n27\t|            4 | NumCyclesIF      | Cycles waiting for instruction fetches, i.e., number of |\n28\t|              |                  | instructions wasted due to non-ideal caching            |\n29\t+--------------+------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+\n30\t|            5 | NumLoads         | Number of data memory loads. Misaligned accesses are    |\n31\t|              |                  | counted as two accesses                                 |\n32\t+--------------+------------------+---------------------------------------------------------+\n33\t|            6 | NumStores        | Number of data memory stores. ``mhpmevent31`` define which of these events are counted by the event counters ``mhpmcounter3(h)`` - ``mhpmcounter31(h)``.\n50\tIf a specific bit in an event selector CSR is set to 1, this means that events with this ID are being counted by the counter associated with that selector CSR.\n51\tIf an event selector CSR is 0, this means that the corresponding counter is not counting any event.\n52\t\n53\tControlling the counters from software\n54\t--------------------------------------\n55\t\n56\tBy default, all available counters are enabled after reset.\n57\tThey can be individually enabled/disabled by overwriting the corresponding bit in the ``mcountinhibit`` CSR at address ``0x320`` as described in the RISC-V Privileged Specification, version 1.11 (see Machine Counter-Inhibit CSR, Section 3.1.13).\n58\tIn particular, to enable/disable ``mcycle(h)``, bit 0 must be written. For ``minstret(h)``, it is bit 2. For event counter ``mhpmcounterX(h)``, it is bit X.\n59\t\n60\tThe lower 32 bits of all counters can be accessed through the base register, whereas the upper 32 bits are accessed through the ``h``-register.\n61\tReads to all these registers are non-destructive.\n62\t\n63\tParametrization at synthesis time\n64\t---------------------------------\n65\t\n66\tThe ``mcycle(h)`` and ``minstret(h)`` counters are always available and 64 bit wide.\n67\t\n68\tThe event counters ``mhpmcounter3(h)`` - ``mhpmcounter31(h)`` are parametrizable.\n69\tTheir width can be parametrized between 1 and 64 bit through the ``WidthMHPMCounters`` parameter, which defaults to 40 bit wide counters.\n70\t\n71\tThe number of available event counters ``mhpmcounterX(h)`` can be controlled via the ``NumMHPMCounters`` parameter.\n72\tBy default (``NumMHPMCounters`` set to 0), no counters are available to software.\n73\tSet ``NumMHPMCounters`` to a value between 1 and 8 to make the counters ``mhpmcounter3(h)`` - ``mhpmcounter10(h)`` available as listed below.\n74\tSetting ``NumMHPMCounters`` to values larger than 8 does not result in any more performance counters.\n75\t\n76\tUnavailable counters always read 0.\n77\t\n78\tThe association of events with the ``mphmcounter`` registers is hardwired as listed in the following table.\n79\t\n80\t+----------------------+----------------+--------------+------------------+\n81\t| Event Counter        | CSR Address    | Event ID/Bit | Event Name Internal Peripheral Details\n\n### `simulator_ctrl` (`/app/shared/rtl/sim/simulator_ctrl.sv`)\n\n```\nCHAR_OUT_ADDR = 8'h0  -> addr_i[9:2] == 0  -> byte addr 0x00 within region\nSIM_CTRL_ADDR = 8'h2  -> addr_i[9:2] == 2  -> byte addr 0x08 within region\n```\n\n- Write to `CHAR_OUT` (offset 0): outputs `wdata_i[7:0]` as a character to a log file.\n- Write `1` to bit 0 of `SIM_CTRL` (offset 8): terminates simulation after 2 cycles (`$finish`).\n- Always responds with `rdata_o = 0`; `rvalid_o` is high the cycle after any `req_i`.\n\nPorts: `clk_i, rst_ni, req_i, we_i, be_i[3:0], addr_i[31:0], wdata_i[31:0], rvalid_o, rdata_o[31:0]`\n\n### `timer` (`/app/shared/rtl/timer.sv`)\n\n- 64-bit `mtime` that increments every clock cycle.\n- 64-bit `mtimecmp`; interrupt fires when `mtime >= mtimecmp`.\n- Interrupt stays asserted until `mtimecmp` is written.\n- Register offsets within the 1 KB window (bits `[9:0]` of address):\n  - `0x0`: MTIME low 32 bits\n  - `0x4`: MTIME high 32 bits\n  - `0x8`: MTIMECMP low\n  - `0xC`: MTIMECMP high\n\nPorts: `clk_i, rst_ni, timer_req_i, timer_addr_i[31:0], timer_we_i, timer_be_i[3:0], timer_wdata_i[31:0], timer_rvalid_o, timer_rdata_o[31:0], timer_err_o, timer_intr_o`\n\n### `bus` (`/app/shared/rtl/bus.sv`)\n\nParameterized interconnect: `NrDevices`, `NrHosts`, `DataWidth=32`, `AddressWidth=32`. Address decode uses `cfg_device_addr_base[NrDevices]` and `cfg_device_addr_mask[NrDevices]`. Priority arbitration (host 0 has lowest priority; highest-indexed wins). Single-cycle response: device must reply in the same cycle the request is presented.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Files in `/app/shared/rtl/`\n\n```\nbus.sv                              - Parameterized bus interconnect\nram_1p.sv                           - Single-port RAM wrapper (wraps prim_ram_1p)\nram_2p.sv                           - Dual-port RAM wrapper (wraps prim_ram_2p)\ntimer.sv                            - RISC-V mtime/mtimecmp timer\nfpga/\n  xilinx/\n    clkgen_xil7series.sv            - Xilinx 7-series clock gen\nsim/\n  simulator_ctrl.sv                 - Simulation control peripheral (char output + halt)\n```\n\n---\n\n## 6. Files in `/app/examples/simple_system/rtl/`\n\n```\nibex_simple_system.sv               - THE FILE YOU MUST IMPLEMENT (currently empty)\n```\n\n---\n\n## 7. `prim_clock_gating.sv` (`/app/vendor/lowrisc_ip/ip/prim_generic/rtl/prim_clock_gating.sv`)\n\n```systemverilog\nmodule prim_clock_gating #(\n  parameter bit NoFpgaGate    = 1'b0,\n  parameter bit FpgaBufGlobal = 1'b1\n) (\n  input        clk_i,\n  input        en_i,\n  input        test_en_i,\n  output logic clk_o\n);\n  logic en_latch /* verilator clock_enable */;\n  always_latch begin\n    if (!clk_i) begin\n      en_latch = en_i | test_en_i;\n    end\n  end\n  assign clk_o = en_latch & clk_i;\nendmodule\n```\n\nA latch-based clock gate: the enable is latched on the low phase of the clock, then ANDed with the clock. The `verilator clock_enable` attribute suppresses Verilator warnings.\n\n---\n\n## 8. `prim_buf.sv` (`/app/vendor/lowrisc_ip/ip/prim_generic/rtl/prim_buf.sv`)\n\n```systemverilog\nmodule prim_buf #(parameter int Width = 1) (\n  input        [Width-1:0] in_i,\n  output logic [Width-1:0] out_o\n);\n  logic [Width-1:0] inv;\n  assign inv   = ~in_i;\n  assign out_o = ~inv;\nendmodule\n```\n\nA double-inverter buffer — synthesis sees it as a real buffer cell; simulation sees pass-through.\n\nNote: `prim_buf.sv` is NOT present under `/app/vendor/lowrisc_ip/ip/prim/rtl/` — it lives in `prim_generic/rtl/` and `prim_xilinx/rtl/`.\n\n---\n\n## 9. `prim_ram_1p.sv` (generic, `/app/vendor/lowrisc_ip/ip/prim_generic/rtl/prim_ram_1p.sv`)\n\nSynchronous single-port SRAM model. Loop through regions 0..PMPNumRegions-1 (highest priority = lowest index)\n2. For each region i, check if the address matches the region:\n   - PMP_MODE_OFF (2'b00): never matches\n   - PMP_MODE_TOR (2'b01): `csr_pmp_addr_i[i-1] <= pmp_req_addr_i[c] < csr_pmp_addr_i[i]` (region 0: 0 <= addr < addr[0])\n   - PMP_MODE_NA4 (2'b10): exact 4-byte alignment match (addr[33:2] == csr_pmp_addr_i[i][33:2])\n   - PMP_MODE_NAPOT (2'b11): natural power-of-2 aligned region; the address register encodes size. The mask is the trailing ones in the address register + 1 bit. Match when `(req_addr & ~mask) == (pmp_addr & ~mask)` where mask is derived from trailing 1s.\n3. If region matches:\n   - In M-mode: access allowed only if `csr_pmp_cfg[i].lock == 0` OR (lock=1 AND R/W/X bit set for request type)\n     - Actually: if lock=1, M-mode is also checked against R/W/X bits. If lock=0, M-mode always allowed\n   - In U-mode: access allowed only if corresponding R/W/X bit is set\n   - MML mode changes permissions - but for basic implementation, handle MML=0 case\n4. If no region matches:\n   - M-mode: allowed (unless mseccfg.mmwp=1)\n   - U-mode: denied\n5. Output `pmp_req_err_o[c] = 1` if access is denied\n\n### NAPOT address decode:\n```\n// Trailing ones in pmp_addr give the log2 of half-region size\n// E.g., addr = 0xXXXXXXFF -> region size = 512 bytes\n// addr = 0xXXXXXX1F -> region size = 64 bytes  \n// Number of trailing ones = n -> size = 2^(n+3) bytes\n// Mask (for address comparison) = ~((1 << (n+1)) - 1) shifted appropriately\n```\n\nFor PMPGranularity > 0, the minimum region size is 2^(PMPGranularity+2) bytes.\n\n### Simple implementation notes:\n- The address registers store `addr[33:2]` (physical address right-shifted by 2)\n- For TOR: compare `pmp_req_addr_i[c][33:2]` against `csr_pmp_addr_i[i][33:2]`\n- The module must be purely combinational (no registers other than potentially for pipeline stages); but the standard Ibex PMP is fully combinational\n- For the basic tests, implement NAPOT and TOR correctly; the pmp_smoke_test exercises these\n\nWrite the complete `/app/rtl/ibex_pmp.sv`. Loop through regions 0..PMPNumRegions-1 (highest priority = lowest index)\n2. For each region i, check if the address matches the region:\n   - PMP_MODE_OFF (2'b00): never matches\n   - PMP_MODE_TOR (2'b01): `csr_pmp_addr_i[i-1] <= pmp_req_addr_i[c] < csr_pmp_addr_i[i]` (region 0: 0 <= addr < addr[0])\n   - PMP_MODE_NA4 (2'b10): exact 4-byte alignment match (addr[33:2] == csr_pmp_addr_i[i][33:2])\n   - PMP_MODE_NAPOT (2'b11): natural power-of-2 aligned region; the address register encodes size. The mask is the trailing ones in the address register + 1 bit. Match when `(req_addr & ~mask) == (pmp_addr & ~mask)` where mask is derived from trailing 1s.\n3. If region matches:\n   - In M-mode: access allowed only if `csr_pmp_cfg[i].lock == 0` OR (lock=1 AND R/W/X bit set for request type)\n     - Actually: if lock=1, M-mode is also checked against R/W/X bits. If lock=0, M-mode always allowed\n   - In U-mode: access allowed only if corresponding R/W/X bit is set\n   - MML mode changes permissions - but for basic implementation, handle MML=0 case\n4. If no region matches:\n   - M-mode: allowed (unless mseccfg.mmwp=1)\n   - U-mode: denied\n5. Output `pmp_req_err_o[c] = 1` if access is denied\n\n### NAPOT address decode:\n```\n// Trailing ones in pmp_addr give the log2 of half-region size\n// E.g., addr = 0xXXXXXXFF -> region size = 512 bytes\n// addr = 0xXXXXXX1F -> region size = 64 bytes  \n// Number of trailing ones = n -> size = 2^(n+3) bytes\n// Mask (for address comparison) = ~((1 << (n+1)) - 1) shifted appropriately\n```\n\nFor PMPGranularity > 0, the minimum region size is 2^(PMPGranularity+2) bytes.\n\n### Simple implementation notes:\n- The address registers store `addr[33:2]` (physical address right-shifted by 2)\n- For TOR: compare `pmp_req_addr_i[c][33:2]` against `csr_pmp_addr_i[i][33:2]`\n- The module must be purely combinational (no registers other than potentially for pipeline stages); but the standard Ibex PMP is fully combinational\n- For the basic tests, implement NAPOT and TOR correctly; the pmp_smoke_test exercises these\n\nWrite the complete `/app/rtl/ibex_pmp.sv`.          |\n11\t+================+===============+==========================================================+\n12\t| PMPEnable      | 0             | PMP support enabled |\n17\t+----------------+---------------+----------------------------------------------------------+\n18\t\n19\tWhen PMPEnable is zero, the PMP module is not instantiated and all PMP registers read as zero (regardless of the value of PMPNumRegions)\n20\t\n21\tPMP Integration\n22\t---------------\n23\t\n24\tAddresses from the instruction fetch unit and load-store unit are passed to the PMP module for checking.\n25\tThe output of PMP check is used to gate the external request of the load-store unit.\n26\tThis is because both writes and reads can have side-effects on MMIO devices connected to the data memory bus.\n27\tThe request coming from the instruction fetch unit are not gated by the PMP check, so integrators must choose carefully what to connect to the instruction fetch bus.\n28\tSpecifically, no devices that experience side-effects due to reading should be available on this bus.\n29\tIn general, connecting memories to the instruction fetch bus should be safe.\n30\t\n31\tTo maintain consistency with external errors, the instruction fetch unit and load-store unit progress with their request as if it was granted externally.\n32\tThe PMP error is address matching comparators by increasing the minimum region size.\n38\tWhen the granularity is greater than zero, NA4 mode is not available and will be treated as OFF mode.\n39\t\n40\t.. configurations which are U-Mode or M-Mode accessible only with varying read/write/execute settings along with some shared U and M mode accessible configurations.\n52\t  These new configurations Let me detail:\n- For ADD: cin=0, adder = a + b\n- For SUB: cin=1, adder = a + ~b + 1 = a - b\n\nThe trick: \n- adder_in_a = {1'b0, operand_a_i}  (33 bits)\n- For ADD: adder_in_b = {1'b0, operand_b_i}, cin=0\n- For SUB: adder_in_b = {1'b0, ~operand_b_i}, cin=1\n\nA simpler approach that works for simulation:\n```systemverilog\nlogic [31:0] adder_op_b;\nassign adder_op_b = adder_op_b_negate ? operand_a_i : {<<{operand_a_i}};  // bit-reverse for left\nassign shift_result_ext = $signed({shift_arith ? shift_operand[31] : 1'b0, shift_operand}) >>> shift_amt;\nassign shift_result = shift_right ? The address register stores addr[33:2] (physical addr >> 2).\n\n## Internal signals needed (referenced by fcov interface)\n\nFrom core_ibex_pmp_fcov_if.sv:\n- `region_match_all[PMPNumChan][PMPNumRegions]` — per-channel, per-region match result\n- `access_fault_check_res[PMPNumChan]` — the raw access fault check result before debug override\n- `region_basic_perm_check[PMPNumChan][PMPNumRegions]` — basic permission check result\n- Functions: `perm_check_wrapper(mml, cfg, req_type, priv_lvl, basic_perm)` — returns logic\n- Functions: `access_fault_check(mmwp, mml, req_type, region_match, priv_lvl, perm_checks)` — returns logic\n\n## Algorithm\n\n### Address Matching\n\nFor each channel c and region i:\n\n**OFF (2'b00):** no_match\n\n**TOR (2'b01):**\n- For region 0: 0 <= req_addr < csr_pmp_addr[0]\n  i.e., req_addr[33:2] < csr_pmp_addr[0][33:2] (lower bound is 0)\n- For region i>0: csr_pmp_addr[i-1][33:2] <= req_addr[33:2] < csr_pmp_addr[i][33:2]\n- With PMPGranularity > 0: mask the lower G bits\n\n**NA4 (2'b10):**\n- Only valid if PMPGranularity == 0; otherwise treated as OFF\n- Match: req_addr[33:2] == csr_pmp_addr[i][33:2]\n\n**NAPOT (2'b11):**\n- Decode trailing ones in csr_pmp_addr[i][33:2] to get mask\n- For PMPGranularity=0: mask = ~( (trailing_ones_mask + 1) ) where trailing_ones_mask is all the trailing 1s\n- Match: (req_addr[33:2] & ~mask[33:2]) == (csr_pmp_addr[i][33:2] & ~mask[33:2])\n- With granularity G: ignore the lower G bits\n\n### NAPOT mask calculation\n\nThe standard approach: find the position of the lowest 0 bit among the trailing 1s in the address register.\n- addr_bits = csr_pmp_addr[i][33:2] (32 bits)\n- napot_mask[j] = &(addr_bits[j:0]) — i.e., 1 if bits 0..j are all ones\n- The mask used for comparison = {napot_mask, 1'b1} — that is: bits below the first 0 (including it) are masked out\n\nMore precisely:\n```\n// For bit position n (0-indexed in the 32-bit addr>>2 field):\n// base_mask[n] = 1 if addr_bits[n-1:0] are all 1s (i.e., position n is the first 0 or above)\n// comparison mask = ~base_mask (keep bits above the region size)\n```\n\nStandard Ibex approach from the spec:\n```\n// napot_mask is a vector where the lowest 0 bit in the address marks the boundary\n// Mask is computed by finding the first 0 bit from LSB\n// napot_mask[i] = addr[i-1:0] == all 1s\n// The compare mask applied to the address is: mask where top bits must match\n```\n\nLet me use the standard approach:\n```\n// addr_base = csr_pmp_addr[i][33:2]  (this is the 32-bit pmpaddr register value)\n// To find mask: identify trailing ones\n// mask_bits[0] = 1 always (bit 0 of addr register is always masked in NAPOT, minimum 8-byte region)\n// mask_bits[j] = mask_bits[j-1] & addr_base[j-1]\n\n// The comparison: (req_addr[33:2] & ~mask_bits) == (addr_base & ~mask_bits)\n// where mask_bits has the bottom (n+1) bits set, n = number of trailing ones\n```\n\nWith PMPGranularity G > 0:\n- The bottom G bits of the comparison address are always masked\n- NA4 becomes OFF\n\n### Permission Check (basic)\n\nFor a matched region i and channel c:\n```\nbasic_perm = (req_type == EXEC)  ? cfg.exec  :\n             (req_type == WRITE) ? cfg.write :\n             (req_type == READ)  ? cfg.read  : 0\n```\n\n### Permission Check with mode and MML\n\n**MML = 0 (standard):**\n- M-mode:\n  - lock=0: always allowed (regardless of R/W/X bits)\n  - lock=1: check R/W/X bits (basic_perm must be 1)\n- U-mode:\n  - always check R/W/X bits (basic_perm must be 1)\n\n**MML = 1 (machine mode lockdown):**\nThe permission semantics are completely different. The {lock, exec, write, read} bits encode a combined M-mode/U-mode permission table:\n\n| L | X | W | R | U-mode         | M-mode         |\n|---|---|---|---|----------------|----------------|\n| 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | ---            | ---            |\n| 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | R              | ---            |\n| 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | R+W (*)        | ---            |\n| 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 | R+W            | ---            |\n| 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | X              | ---            |\n| 0 | 1 | 0 | 1 | X+R            | ---            |\n| 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | R+W+X (*)      | ---            |\n| 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 | R+W+X          | ---            |\n| 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | ---            | ---            |\n| 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 | ---            | R              |\n| 1 | 0 | 1 | 0 | ---            | X+R/U sharing (*)|\n| 1 | 0 | 1 | 1 | ---            | R+W            |\n| 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | ---            | X              |\n| 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | ---            | X+R            |\n| 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | X+R            | X+R/U sharing  |\n| 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | R              | R+W            |\n\nThis is the Smepmp table. To implement properly we need the exact permission table.\n\n### No-match default\n\nIf no region matches channel c:\n- M-mode: allow unless mseccfg.mmwp=1 OR mseccfg.mml=1 \n  - Actually with mml=1, M-mode no-match is also deny\n- U-mode: always deny\n\nMore precisely from the Smepmp spec:\n- No match, M-mode, mml=0, mmwp=0: allow\n- No match, M-mode, mml=0, mmwp=1: deny\n- No match, M-mode, mml=1: deny (no shared region)\n- No match, U-mode: always deny\n\n### Debug Module override\n\nThe fcov references `access_fault_check_res` which is the fault result before debug override. However, looking at the interface, the module has no debug_mode input — so the debug override is probably handled in ibex_core's g_pmp wrapper, not inside ibex_pmp itself.\n\nLooking at the fcov interface more carefully:\n- `access_fault_check_res` is what the PMP computes internally\n- `pmp_req_err_o` (the output) might incorporate debug override\n- But ibex_pmp's interface has no debug_mode signal\n\nSo `access_fault_check_res` == `pmp_req_err_o` for this module. u_w=1; u_x=0; m_r=1; m_w=1; m_x=0; end  // U:RW, M:RW (shared)\n      4'b1100: begin u_r=0; u_w=0; u_x=0; m_r=1; m_w=1; m_x=1; end  // M:RWX only\n      4'b1101: begin u_r=0; u_w=0; u_x=0; m_r=1; m_w=0; m_x=1; end  // M:RX only\n      4'b1110: begin u_r=1; u_w=0; u_x=1; m_r=1; m_w=1; m_x=1; end  // U:RX, M:RWX (shared)\n      4'b1111: begin u_r=1; u_w=0; u_x=0; m_r=1; m_w=1; m_x=0; end  // U:R, M:RW\n      default: begin u_r=0; u_w=0; u_x=0; m_r=0; m_w=0; m_x=0; end\n    endcase\n    if (priv_lvl == PRIV_LVL_M) begin\n      unique case (req_type)\n        PMP_ACC_EXEC:  return m_x;\n        PMP_ACC_WRITE: return m_w;\n        PMP_ACC_READ:  return m_r;\n        default:       return 1'b0;\n      endcase\n    end else begin\n      unique case (req_type)\n        PMP_ACC_EXEC:  return u_x;\n        PMP_ACC_WRITE: return u_w;\n        PMP_ACC_READ:  return u_r;\n        default:       return 1'b0;\n      endcase\n    end\n  endfunction\n\n  // access_fault_check: given all region matches and perm checks,\n  // return 1 if access should be faulted\n  function automatic logic access_fault_check(\n    logic                        mmwp,\n    logic                        mml,\n    pmp_req_e                    req_type,\n    logic [PMPNumRegions-1:0]    region_match,\n    priv_lvl_e                   priv_lvl,\n    logic [PMPNumRegions-1:0]    perm_check_vec\n  );\n    logic matched;\n    logic permitted;\n    matched  = |region_match;\n    // Find highest priority match (lowest index) and check its permissions\n    permitted = 1'b0;\n    for (int i = PMPNumRegions-1; The `napot_mask` indexing: the pmpaddr register stores addr[33:2]. So pmpaddr[0] corresponds to physical address bit 2. The NAPOT encoding uses trailing 1s in the pmpaddr value. For 8-byte region: pmpaddr = xxxxxx0 (no trailing 1s needed, minimum). Wait, actually:\n   - Minimum NAPOT = 8 bytes. pmpaddr stores addr[33:2]. For an 8-byte aligned region of 8 bytes, the low bit of pmpaddr is don't-care (not encoded as 1, just masked).\n   - For 16 bytes: pmpaddr[0] = 1, pmpaddr[1:0] stores any value (bit 0 = 1 means 16-byte)\n   - For 32 bytes: pmpaddr[1:0] = 11, so 2 trailing 1s\n   - For 64 bytes: pmpaddr[2:0] = 111\n   - So: n trailing 1s in pmpaddr → region size = 2^(n+3) bytes\n   - napot_mask bit j = 1 if j <= n (bits 0..n are the \"trailing ones\" region)\n   - napot_mask[0] is always 1 (minimum 8 bytes, bit 0 is always masked)\n   \n   The mask for comparison: bits [j:0] of pmpaddr are masked when comparing with req_addr[33:2].\n   \n   So: napot_mask[i][0] = 1'b1 always\n   napot_mask[i][j] = napot_mask[i][j-1] & pmpaddr[i][j-1+2]   (because pmpaddr[33:2] is the reg value, so bit j of the register is at pmpaddr[j+2])\n   \n   Wait - pmpaddr[i] IS already the 34-bit value `{addr[33:2], 2'b00}` based on the interface description: `input logic [33:0] csr_pmp_addr_i`. So csr_pmp_addr_i[i] is the 34-bit value where bits [33:2] hold the pmpaddr register value and bits [1:0] are 0.\n   \n   Actually looking at the interface description more carefully: \"The address registers store addr[33:2] (physical address right-shifted by 2)\". So csr_pmp_addr_i[i][33:2] = pmpaddr register value, and csr_pmp_addr_i[i][1:0] = 0.\n   \n   For NAPOT mask calculation:\n   - pmpaddr_reg[j] = csr_pmp_addr_i[i][j+2] for j in 0..31\n   - napot_mask_bit[j] = 1 means bit j of pmpaddr_reg (= addr bit j+2) is \"don't care\"\n   - napot_mask_bit[0] = 1 always\n   - napot_mask_bit[j] = napot_mask_bit[j-1] & pmpaddr_reg[j-1] = napot_mask_bit[j-1] & csr_pmp_addr_i[i][j+1]\n   \n   Full 34-bit mask (including the 2 low bits):\n   - napot_mask[i][0] = 1'b1 (addr[0] always masked)\n   - napot_mask[i][1] = 1'b1 (addr[1] always masked) \n   - napot_mask[i][2] = 1'b1 (pmpaddr bit 0 always masked for min 8-byte region)\n   - napot_mask[i][3] = csr_pmp_addr_i[i][2] (if pmpaddr[0]=1, 16-byte)\n   - napot_mask[i][j] for j>=3 = napot_mask[i][j-1] & csr_pmp_addr_i[i][j-1]\n\n2. For TOR with PMPGranularity: the comparison should mask the lower G bits in the address. The standard approach is to zero out the lower G bits of both bounds and the request address before comparing.\n\n3. The `access_fault_check` function priority: lower index = higher priority. So we iterate from 0 to PMPNumRegions-1, and the LAST match (highest-priority = lowest index) overrides. To implement \"first match wins\" (lowest index), we should iterate from high to low and take the last hit:\n   ```\n   permitted = default_no_match_value;\n   for i from high to low:\n     if region_match[i]:\n       permitted = perm_check[i]\n   ```\n   This way region 0 (highest priority) overwrites everything.\n\n## Final plan summary\n\nWrite `/app/rtl/ibex_pmp.sv` with:\n1.
